name: Hannah Arendt
worldviewSummary: Arendt distinguishes labor (sustaining biological life), work (fabricating a durable world) and action (initiating something new among plural equals through speech). Modern society tends to reduce all activity to labor and consumption. Her analysis of Eichmann introduced the 'banality of evil': great wrongs committed through thoughtlessness rather than demonic motives.
biography: German-born Jewish political theorist who fled Nazi Germany, was interned in France, and emigrated to the United States in 1941. Author of The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951), The Human Condition (1958) and Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963). She rejected the label 'philosopher', preferring 'political theorist'.

works.title: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil

concepts.description: The vita activa comprises labor (the cyclical maintenance of life), work (the making of durable things) and action (beginning something new in the plural public realm).
Eichmann appeared not monstrous but thoughtless — terrifyingly normal, speaking in clichés, unable to think from another's standpoint.
Because each person is a new beginning, human beings are capable of action that starts something unprecedented.

positions.statement: The prospect of automation threatens a society of laborers freed from labor who no longer know the higher activities for whose sake that freedom would be worth winning.
Thoughtlessness — the failure to stop and think about what one is doing — can enable participation in great crimes without wicked intent.
Freedom is experienced in action among equals in a shared public world; its loss leaves people isolated, which totalitarianism exploits.
Technical capabilities may outstrip our capacity to think and speak about what we are doing, so such questions must be political, not left to experts.

relations.note: Diverged from her former teacher philosophically and politically.
The Human Condition criticizes Marx's elevation of labor.
